items.stem: Which term describes an informal, guided conversation with no fixed list of questions, allowing the interviewee to talk freely?
items.answer: Unstructured interview
items.markingKey: Unstructured interview: an informal, guided conversation with no fixed list of questions, allowing the interviewee to talk freely. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “semi-structured interview”, and give one example.
items.answer: An interview with a set of core questions but freedom for the interviewer to probe and ask follow-up questions. Example: asking every teacher the same five questions and then following up interesting answers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (an interview with a set of core questions but freedom for the interviewer to probe and ask follow-up questions); 1 mark for a relevant example such as asking every teacher the same five questions and then following up interesting answers. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “transcript” and “group interview”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Transcript: a written record of everything said in an interview (e.g. a typed record of a recorded interview). Group interview: an interview with several people at once, in which they can discuss topics with one another (e.g. interviewing a group of five friends together).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Mateo spends three hours talking to a woman in Jakarta who has left a violent partner, letting her tell her story in her own way. Suggest how an interpretivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: social reality is constructed through the meanings people give to their actions, so researchers must use qualitative methods such as unstructured interviews and participant observation to achieve verstehen and valid data (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Dubai interviews groups of five teenage boys about their views on masculinity and notices that one boy dominates each discussion. Explain how an interpretivist sociologist might evaluate this research.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research women’s experiences of domestic violence.
items.answer: Strengths: anonymity may encourage respondents to admit sensitive or embarrassing behaviour they would not reveal face to face; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying women’s experiences of domestic violence but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “transcript”.

items.stem: Source A: “A sociologist interviewed 20 fathers in Lagos who had taken more than six months of parental leave. Each interview lasted around two hours and followed the father’s own account. Many said they had felt “out of place” at parent groups, and several said friends had questioned their masculinity.” Use Source A and your own knowledge to answer the questions. (a) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that unstructured interviews are the best method for studying family life.
items.answer: (a) 1. Many fathers felt out of place at parent groups. 2. Several said friends had questioned their masculinity. (b) For: The source shows rich, detailed data on feelings and meanings, gained through long interviews following the fathers’ own accounts. Against: Twenty fathers in one city cannot be generalised; interviews record what people say rather than what they do; time-use diaries or questionnaires show wider patterns; interviewer effects may shape answers. Also consider how far a single study using unstructured interviews can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “participant observation”, and give one example.

items.stem: Distinguish between “gatekeeper” and “going native”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Gatekeeper: a person who controls access to a group or setting (e.g. a gang leader who introduces the researcher to members). Going native: becoming so involved with the group being studied that the researcher loses objectivity (e.g. a researcher adopting the group’s values and defending its actions).

items.stem: Felix, a sociology lecturer in Kathmandu, takes a job in a fast-food restaurant without telling colleagues, to study how workers cope with boring work. Explain how feminist and positivist sociologists might differ in the way they evaluate this research.

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of non-participant observation for studying a religious sect in Dhaka.
items.answer: Strengths: the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively; a structured observation schedule allows behaviour to be counted and compared, improving reliability. Limitations: the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect); the researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying a religious sect in Dhaka but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using participant observation to research interaction in primary school classrooms.
items.answer: Strengths: it records real behaviour, avoiding the gap between what people say and what they do; it is flexible and can uncover issues the researcher had not anticipated. Limitations: the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt; the researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”). Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying interaction in primary school classrooms but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “covert observation” and “non-participant observation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Covert observation: observation in which the group does not know that it is being studied (e.g. a researcher posing as a member of a religious group). Non-participant observation: a method in which the researcher observes a group without taking part in its activities (e.g. a researcher sitting at the back of a classroom).

items.stem: Source A: “A researcher worked for eight months as a part-time cleaner in a large hotel in Muscat without telling her colleagues she was a sociologist. She found that cleaners helped each other to meet impossible targets and used humour to cope with rude guests. She wrote her notes each evening from memory.” Use Source A and your own knowledge to answer the questions. (a) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying workplace culture among hotel cleaners. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that covert participant observation is the best way to study workplace culture.
items.answer: (a) It involves deception and lack of informed consent, which breaks ethical guidelines. (b) For: The source shows natural behaviour observed over a long period; colleagues did not know they were being studied, avoiding the Hawthorne effect. Against: There was no informed consent; notes written from memory may be inaccurate; one hotel may be untypical; overt observation or interviews avoid deception. Also consider how far a single study using covert participant observation can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying how children’s family circumstances affect their later lives.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how children’s family circumstances affect their later lives but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).

Many said they had felt “out of place” at parent groups, and several said friends had questioned their masculinity.” Use Source A and your own knowledge to answer the questions. (a) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying fathers’ experiences of parental leave. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that unstructured interviews are the best method for studying family life.
items.answer: (a) Each interview is unique, so it is hard to repeat and the data is less reliable. (b) For: The source shows rich, detailed data on feelings and meanings, gained through long interviews following the fathers’ own accounts. Against: Twenty fathers in one city cannot be generalised; interviews record what people say rather than what they do; time-use diaries or questionnaires show wider patterns; interviewer effects may shape answers. Also consider how far a single study using unstructured interviews can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes observation in which the group knows that the researcher is studying them?
items.answer: Overt observation
items.markingKey: Overt observation: observation in which the group knows that the researcher is studying them. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “field notes”.
items.answer: The written record a researcher makes of observations during or after fieldwork.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the written record a researcher makes of observations during or after fieldwork. [1]

items.stem: Explain two problems a researcher might face in getting into, staying in and getting out of a group.
items.answer: Getting in: gaining access and trust, especially through gatekeepers; staying in: risk of going native or being discovered, recording data; getting out: leaving may be difficult or dangerous and relationships end.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained problem. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Muscat wants to research interaction in primary school classrooms. Explain one strength of using self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: They can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of interaction in primary school classrooms. [2]

items.stem: Tariq, a sociology lecturer in Mumbai, takes a job in a fast-food restaurant without telling colleagues, to study how workers cope with boring work. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: sociology should study society scientifically, using quantitative, reliable methods such as questionnaires and official statistics to discover social facts, correlations and causes; the researcher should remain objective and detached (Comte, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Read Source A. “A researcher worked for eight months as a part-time cleaner in a large hotel in Colombo without telling her colleagues she was a sociologist. She found that cleaners helped each other to meet impossible targets and used humour to cope with rude guests. She wrote her notes each evening from memory.” (a) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying workplace culture among hotel cleaners. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that covert participant observation is the best way to study workplace culture.
items.answer: (a) The researcher may be drawn into illegal or harmful activity and is at risk if discovered. (b) For: The source shows natural behaviour observed over a long period; colleagues did not know they were being studied, avoiding the Hawthorne effect. Against: There was no informed consent; notes written from memory may be inaccurate; one hotel may be untypical; overt observation or interviews avoid deception. Also consider how far a single study using covert participant observation can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying interaction in primary school classrooms.
items.answer: Strengths: they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying interaction in primary school classrooms but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes documents produced by organisations such as governments, schools and businesses?
items.answer: Public documents
items.markingKey: Public documents: documents produced by organisations such as governments, schools and businesses. [1]

items.stem: Explain two problems of using personal documents in sociological research.
items.answer: Authenticity: they may be fake or altered; credibility: writers may exaggerate or present themselves favourably; representativeness: only some people keep or publish documents; meaning: interpretation may be difficult.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained problem. [4]

items.stem: Mohammed studies hundreds of social media posts written by young climate activists in Kathmandu to understand why they joined the movement. Suggest how a feminist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Feminism: research has often ignored women’s experiences; feminist researchers prefer non-hierarchical, qualitative methods that give women a voice and take account of power relationships in research (Oakley).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A research team in Dhaka has followed 5,000 children born in the same week since 2000, interviewing them every few years. Explain how an interpretivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: social reality is constructed through the meanings people give to their actions, so researchers must use qualitative methods such as unstructured interviews and participant observation to achieve verstehen and valid data (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of case studies for studying how children’s family circumstances affect their later lives.
items.answer: Strengths: they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples; they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community. Limitations: a single case cannot show how widespread a pattern is; the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how children’s family circumstances affect their later lives but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: State one way in which mixed methods can improve sociological research.
items.answer: Triangulation checks validity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. triangulation checks validity. [1]

items.stem: Explain Hey’s argument that girls’ friendships can be studied through a combination of observation and their own notes, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Valerie Hey combined observation in schools with analysis of notes passed between girls to study their friendships. Criticism: The notes were obtained without full consent of all writers, raising ethical issues.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Liberal feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Lina finds that interview data about how often teachers praise pupils does not match what she observed in their lessons. Suggest how a positivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Positivism: sociology should study society scientifically, using quantitative, reliable methods such as questionnaires and official statistics to discover social facts, correlations and causes; the researcher should remain objective and detached (Comte, Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]
